sections.b: Jubilees, a retelling of Genesis that the Ethiopian Orthodox churches count as Scripture, fills the silence of Genesis 11 with a boyhood. At fourteen Abram sees through the idols, parts from his father's worship and prays to the Creator (Jubilees 11:16–17). He drives off the ravens Mastema sent against the crops and invents a seed box for the plow (Jubilees 11:18–24). He pleads with Terah, burns the house of idols, gives up reading the stars, and only then hears God's call (Jubilees 12:1–24). The book also leaves out Abram's lie about Sarai in Egypt and Gerar (Jubilees 13:11; 16:10), making him a model without fault.
sections.refs: Jubilees 11:16–24; Jubilees 12:1–24; Jubilees 13:11; Jubilees 16:10; Genesis 12:1; Joshua 24:2–3

uncommon: Jubilees has Abram learn Hebrew, "the language of creation," from an angel, and copy his fathers' books (Jubilees 12:25–27).

sections.h: How idol worship began, in Jubilees
sections.b: Jubilees tells a story the Bible does not: after the Flood, Noah's descendants made molten and carved images, and "cruel spirits" sent by Prince Mastema helped them and led them astray (Jubilees 11:4–5). Serug and Nahor worship idols and learn the Chaldeans' omens (Jubilees 11:7–8). Abram's speech to Terah gathers the prophets' arguments: idols have no spirit, must be carried on shoulders, and bring shame, while God sends the rain (Jubilees 12:2–5; Isaiah 46:7; Jeremiah 10:5; Jeremiah 14:22). Then Abram burns the house of idols (Jubilees 12:12).
sections.refs: Jubilees 11:4–8; Jubilees 12:1–14; Joshua 24:2; Isaiah 46:1–7; Jeremiah 10:1–16; 1 Corinthians 10:20

sections.h: Abram's tithe as a law forever (Jubilees)
sections.b: In Jubilees Abram's tenth to Melchizedek (only in bracketed words of VanderKam's Ge'ez text; the manuscripts Charles used have a gap) becomes "an ordinance forever": a first tithe of grain, wine, oil, cattle and sheep, given to "the priests who serve before him," to eat and drink with joy before the Lord (Jubilees 13:25–27). The book later adds a second tithe eaten before the Lord each year (Jubilees 32:10–11). Tobit also gives a tenth to the Levites and spends a second tenth in Jerusalem, with a third-year gift for orphans, widows and converts (Tobit 1:7–8). Hebrews uses the same story to argue that Melchizedek's priesthood is greater than Levi's (Hebrews 7:4–10).
sections.refs: Jubilees 13:25–27; Jubilees 32:10–11; Genesis 14:20; Numbers 18:21–26; Deuteronomy 14:22–27; Tobit 1:7–8; Hebrews 7:4–10

sections.b: Jubilees retells Genesis 14 but, in the manuscripts R. H. Charles used, breaks off just where Melchizedek should appear (Jubilees 13:25). VanderKam's critical Ge'ez text (1989) prints words in square brackets that fill the gap: Abram killed Chedorlaomer, came back, and gave Melchizedek a tenth of everything. Charles 1902 called the gap an obvious lacuna. So the oldest full witness to Jubilees cannot tell us whether the book first named the priest-king.
sections.refs: Jubilees 13:24–25; Genesis 14:17–20; Hebrews 7:1–10

sections.h: The eighth day and the angels (Jubilees 15)
sections.b: Jubilees retells Genesis 17 and then makes the eighth day absolute: "The days may not be cut short, and not one day of the eight may be passed over," because the law is written on the heavenly tablets (Jubilees 15:25). A boy not circumcised by the eighth day belongs "to the children of destruction" (Jubilees 15:26). The highest angels were created circumcised, and Israel is made holy to be with them (Jubilees 15:27). The angel foretells that Israel will neglect the rite and become like the nations, with no pardon (Jubilees 15:33–34). Charles 1902 read this against the crisis of 1 Maccabees 1:15 and 1:48. Isaac is "the first to be circumcised by the covenant" on the eighth day (Jubilees 16:14).
sections.refs: Jubilees 15:11–34; Jubilees 16:14; Genesis 17:9–14; Leviticus 12:3; 1 Maccabees 1:15; 1 Maccabees 1:48; Romans 2:28–29; Acts 15:1–20

common: Jubilees insists on the eighth day without exception, a stricter rule than the later Mishnah's.

sections.b: Jubilees says Abraham was "the first to keep the Feast of Booths on the earth" (Jubilees 16:21). In the seventh month, at the Well of the Oath, he built booths for himself and his servants, offered burnt offerings, a goat for sin, a peace offering and incense of seven spices, and every day walked around the altar seven times with palm fronds (Jubilees 16:20–31). The feast is "the feast of the Lord," kept in joy for the promised son, with no foreigner or uncircumcised man present (Jubilees 16:25–27). The heavenly tablets then make it a law for Israel forever, with booths, wreaths, branches and willows (Jubilees 16:29–30). Leviticus instead ties the booths to the wilderness (Leviticus 23:43).
sections.refs: Jubilees 16:20–31; Leviticus 23:33–43; Numbers 29:12–38; Deuteronomy 16:13–15; Nehemiah 8:14–18; John 7:2; John 7:37

sections.h: Abram's covenants and the Feast of Weeks (Jubilees 14–16)
sections.b: Jubilees dates the covenant between the pieces to the middle of the third month and says it was made like Noah's covenant "in this month"; Abram "renewed the feast" (Jubilees 14:1, 10, 20). Abram keeps "the feast of the firstfruits of the wheat harvest" in the middle of the third month (Jubilees 15:1), and Isaac is born on it (Jubilees 16:13). Charles 1902 argued that the book kept the Feast of Weeks on the fifteenth of the third month, unlike the Pharisees' sixth, because it read "the day after the Sabbath" in Leviticus 23:15 in yet another way.
sections.refs: Jubilees 14:1; Jubilees 14:10; Jubilees 14:20; Jubilees 15:1–2; Jubilees 16:13; Exodus 34:22; Leviticus 23:15–21; Acts 2:1

sections.h: Nations under spirits, Israel under God (Jubilees 15)
sections.b: Jubilees says that over every nation God "set spirits in power, to lead them astray from him," but over Israel "he set no one in power, no angel and no spirit, because he alone is their ruler" (Jubilees 15:31–32). It builds on Deuteronomy 32:8–9 and stands beside Sirach 17:17, but differs from Daniel, where Michael is Israel's prince (Daniel 10:21; Daniel 12:1). Charles 1902 compared Paul's "basic elements of the world" (Galatians 4:3).
sections.refs: Jubilees 15:30–32; Deuteronomy 32:8–9; Sirach 17:17; Daniel 10:13; Daniel 10:20–21; Galatians 4:3

sections.b: In Jubilees, Prince Mastema, the chief of the evil spirits left on earth after the Flood (Jubilees 10:8–9), works hard to spread war, bloodshed and idolatry, sending out the spirits "put under his hand" (Jubilees 11:4–5). He sends ravens to eat the seed and starve the land (Jubilees 11:11). The book never calls him Satan, but he plays the accuser's role, and Charles 1902 compares the Talmud's story in which Satan prompts Abraham's test. Jubilees also speaks of "sons of Beliar" (Jubilees 15:33), as Paul names Beliar (2 Corinthians 6:15).
sections.refs: Jubilees 11:4–5; Jubilees 11:11; Jubilees 15:33; Job 1:6–12; 2 Corinthians 6:15

sections.b: Jubilees retells the fall of Sodom, Gomorrah and Zeboiim in one verse and names their sin: they were cruel, made themselves unclean and "committed sexual sin in their flesh" (Jubilees 16:5). It then makes Sodom a law: the Lord will judge in the same way "the places where people act like Sodom in its impurity" (Jubilees 16:6). This is close to Jude 7, while Ezekiel 16:49–50 puts pride and neglect of the poor first.
sections.refs: Jubilees 16:5–6; Genesis 19:24–25; Ezekiel 16:49–50; Jude 7; 2 Peter 2:6; Luke 17:28–30

sections.b: Jubilees leaves out the quarrel of the herders (Jubilees 13:17) and says Lot was saved only "because the Lord remembered Abraham" (Jubilees 16:7). It then blames Lot with his daughters for a sin not done "from the days of Adam," and says the heavenly tablets doom all his offspring (Jubilees 16:8–9). Genesis puts the plan on the daughters (Genesis 19:31–35), 2 Peter calls Lot righteous (2 Peter 2:7), and Ruth the Moabite enters David's line (Ruth 4:17).
sections.refs: Jubilees 13:17–18; Jubilees 16:7–9; Genesis 19:29–38; 2 Peter 2:7; Deuteronomy 2:9; Ruth 4:17

sections.b: In Jubilees Abraham rejoices rather than laughs at the promise (Jubilees 15:17), Isaac's name is "set and written on the heavenly tablets" (Jubilees 16:3), and he is born in the middle of the third month, on the feast of the firstfruits (Jubilees 16:13). He is "the first to be circumcised by the covenant" on the eighth day (Jubilees 16:14), and through him alone, and then through one of his sons, comes "a holy offspring" (Jubilees 16:16–18).
sections.refs: Jubilees 15:15–21; Jubilees 16:1–4; Jubilees 16:12–18; Genesis 17:15–21; Genesis 21:1–5; Romans 9:7

sections.b: Jubilees calls Sarai "his father's daughter," following Abraham's words in Genesis 20:12, and dates the marriage to the fortieth jubilee (Jubilees 12:9). The Ge'ez calls her Sora until God renames her Sarah (Jubilees 15:15). The book leaves out Abram's request that she call herself his sister (Jubilees 13:11; compare Genesis 12:11–13).
sections.refs: Jubilees 12:9; Jubilees 13:11–15; Jubilees 15:15–16; Jubilees 16:1–3; Genesis 20:12; Leviticus 18:9

sections.h: Hebrew lost at Babel and given back to Abram (Jubilees 12)
sections.b: Jubilees says the revealed language "had ceased from the mouths of all humankind since the day of the overthrow" of the tower, until an angel opened Abram's mouth and spoke with him "in Hebrew, in the language of creation" (Jubilees 12:25–26). George Syncellus quotes the line in Greek. Another early view, which Charles 1902 found in Augustine (City of God 16.11) and others, held that Eber kept Hebrew because he did not help build the tower.
sections.refs: Jubilees 10:26; Jubilees 12:25–27; Genesis 11:1–9; Zephaniah 3:9

sections.b: Raised among Chaldeans who read omens in the sky (Jubilees 11:8), Abram sits up on the first night of the seventh month to learn the coming rains from the stars. A word comes into his heart: "All the signs of the stars and the signs of the moon and the sun are in the Lord's hand. Why am I searching them out?" (Jubilees 12:16–18). Charles 1902 notes a rabbinic story with the same point, in which God tells Abram he is a prophet, not a star-gazer (Genesis Rabbah 44).
sections.refs: Jubilees 11:8; Jubilees 12:16–18; Genesis 1:14; Deuteronomy 4:19; Jeremiah 10:2; Isaiah 47:13–14

sections.b: Jubilees narrows God's choice step by step. God "did not bring Ishmael, his sons, his brothers or Esau near to himself," but "chose Israel to be his people" (Jubilees 15:30). Of Isaac's sons only one will be "a holy offspring," the share of the Most High, "a kingdom, a priesthood and a holy people" (Jubilees 16:17–18; Exodus 19:6). Paul uses the same narrowing to show that God's choice is by his call, not by birth (Romans 9:6–13), and then opens it to Gentiles by faith (Galatians 3:7–9).
sections.refs: Jubilees 15:30–32; Jubilees 16:16–18; Exodus 19:5–6; Romans 9:6–13; 1 Peter 2:9

sections.h: Angels in the story of Abraham (Jubilees 12–16)
sections.b: In Jubilees the narrating angel of the presence carries God's call to Abram ("through me," Jubilees 12:22) and teaches him Hebrew (Jubilees 12:25–27). The highest two orders of angels were created circumcised (Jubilees 15:27). At Mamre it is "we," the angels, who appear and speak, and no meal is eaten (Jubilees 16:1–4).
sections.refs: Jubilees 12:22–27; Jubilees 15:27; Jubilees 16:1–4; Galatians 3:19; Hebrews 13:2

sections.b: Jubilees tells how Prince Mastema sent ravens to eat the seed in the fields of the Chaldeans, so that Terah got his name from the poverty they caused, and how the boy Abram turned the clouds of ravens back seventy times in one day (Jubilees 11:11–21). Jerome knew the story and cites an apocryphal Genesis for it (Letter 78, as quoted in Charles 1902).
sections.refs: Jubilees 11:11–24; Numbers 33:27; Genesis 15:11

sections.h: Ur, Kesed and the Chaldeans' lore (Jubilees 11)
sections.b: Jubilees explains "Ur of the Chaldeans" by an ancestor: Ur son of Kesed built the city and named it after himself and his father (Jubilees 11:3). Nahor learns from his father "the studies of the Chaldeans, how to tell the future and read omens by the signs in the sky" (Jubilees 11:8), the lore Abram later leaves behind (Jubilees 12:16–18).
sections.refs: Jubilees 11:3; Jubilees 11:7–8; Jubilees 12:16–18; Genesis 11:28; Daniel 2:2

sections.h: Laws, names and judgments on the tablets (Jubilees 15–16)
sections.b: In chapters 15 and 16 of Jubilees the heavenly tablets hold three kinds of things. A law: eighth-day circumcision is "an eternal ordinance, set and written on the heavenly tablets" (Jubilees 15:25), and so is the Feast of Booths (Jubilees 16:29). A name: Isaac's, "as it is set and written on the heavenly tablets" before his birth (Jubilees 16:3). A judgment: the doom of Lot's offspring is "commanded and engraved on the heavenly tablets" (Jubilees 16:9). Abraham keeps his feast "as the testimony of the heavenly tablets says" (Jubilees 16:28).
sections.refs: Jubilees 15:25; Jubilees 16:3; Jubilees 16:9; Jubilees 16:28–29; Luke 10:20
